title: Hosted API: Chat demo — params, streaming and recovery patterns
summary: Intro to Redwood hosted chat API focusing on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and recovery/fallback strategies. Customer concerned about cost and latency tradeoffs; SE demoed streaming SDK, backoff/retry patterns, and prefix caching. Agreed next steps: run a short benchmark, share security docs, and schedule a POC kickoff next week.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-11-01 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee, Priya Kapoor, Marta Ruiz (Redwood) — Marcus Chen, Lina Gomez, Aisha Patel, Noah Rivera (BlueCanvas)

Summary note: Quick demo focusing on hosted chat API streaming behavior and recovery playbook, with some discussion on cost/latency tradeoffs and enterprise constraints.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood team, and with me is Priya our SE. Quick intros?
[00:08] Marcus Chen: Marcus here, CTO at BlueCanvas — we'll be evaluating chat on our customer support flow.
[00:12] Lina Gomez: Lina, lead ML engineer, I'll be running the integration.
[00:15] Aisha Patel: Aisha, SRE, I'll cover networking and security questions.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: Great. Quick agenda: show hosted chat basics, streaming demo, then retry and fallback patterns and console hints for cost. Sound ok?
[00:28] Noah Rivera: Yep, fine.
[00:31] Priya Kapoor: Ok jumping in, I'll share my screen — showing a simple SDK snippet calling /v1/chat with streaming enabled. We include a system prompt, some recent user messages, and then we stream tokens back. Notice here we've set temperature 0.2 and top_p 0.9 for more determinism.
[00:48] [screen share noise] Priya Kapoor: streaming means you get partial deltas as soon as the model emits them, so lower perceived latency for UX. If we switched to non-streaming the whole response comes at once.
[01:05] Lina Gomez: Is streaming always cheaper? or does it affect billing?
[01:09] Priya Kapoor: Billing is per token generated/consumed same either way, so streaming doesn't change unit cost, but it can reduce perceived latency and let you early-abort in some flows which saves tokens. The main cost levers are max_tokens, prompt size, and model family.
[01:22] Marcus Chen: For our support use case we have lots of short messages but some long context — how do you handle long histories?
[01:28] Priya Kapoor: Two things — KV/prefix caching and truncation strategies. Redwood supports automatic prefix caching for repeated system/context so you avoid re-sending large static prompts. Also you can use our console to view token distribution per route. Note: sometimes transcriber says K V cash which is actually KV cache, apologies.
[01:44] Jordan Lee: Quick demo of retry pattern — we recommend idempotency keys for non-streaming calls and a streaming reconnection strategy for intermittent network failures. Priya show the reconnection?
[01:52] Priya Kapoor: Sure. So streaming reconnection: on an aborted stream we re-open with the same conversation state and the runtime will resume using the last committed kv pointer—there's a small overlap risk so dedupe client-side is recommended. We show an example of exponential backoff with jitter: 500ms, 1s, 2s, capped at 8s.
[02:12] Aisha Patel: Do you have guidance for when to fall back to a smaller cheaper model automatically?
[02:16] Priya Kapoor: Yes, the smart routing policy can fallback by cost tier or region. We demo policy rules in the console: if P50 latency exceeds X ms or error rate > 2% then route to model-compact-v1. Note the tradeoff on quality.
[02:28] Marcus Chen: How invasive is the SDK change? We use a node lambda for web chat.
[02:32] Jordan Lee: It's a single dependency plus env var for API key. For streaming we provide server-side and browser-friendly options; our browser token minting guide avoids leaking keys. We'll share the quickstart repo.
[02:41] Lina Gomez: Ok show us a live run with a real-ish sample.
[02:44] Priya Kapoor: Running now — sample payload from support logs (anonymized). Starting stream...
[02:50] [demo audio] Priya Kapoor: (typing) token stream incoming... first chunk: "Hi I can help you with..." next chunk completes with steps. You can see partials arriving within 80–120ms per chunk in this setup.
[03:10] Lina Gomez: That's good. What's your default chunk size?
[03:12] Priya Kapoor: We stream at sub-token or token boundaries depending on model; chunk timing varies by model perf. For our benchmarks we often see 30–70ms per token on dedicated hardware but hosted multi-tenant varies.
[03:27] Marcus Chen: Latency numbers — p50 p95?
[03:29] Priya Kapoor: For this model on hosted in us-west: P50 ~120ms for first chunk, P95 ~900ms for longer responses under load. We'll run an isolated benchmark with your payloads to get a more accurate picture.
[03:41] Noah Rivera: About cost — how would you recommend capping tokens for our flow?
[03:45] Priya Kapoor: Use max_tokens plus dynamic truncation of older context. Also use stop sequences and conservative temperature to avoid verbosity. You can also set token_budget per conversation and enforce server-side.
[03:55] Marcus Chen: Ok, now failures — what's a typical recovery sequence on a stream error?
[03:59] Priya Kapoor: Detect close event, snapshot last acked token index, backoff, re-open with same conversation id and ack index. If repeated failures fallback to non-streaming sync call to ensure completion. We also recommend a canary route to a smaller model to keep UX alive.
[04:14] Aisha Patel: How does session affinity work? we need to pin to zones for compliance?
[04:18] Marta Ruiz: We support affinity by region and deployment type. For strict residency use Redwood Private or dedicated pools, else hosted region pinning is available. There are also VPC-peering options for dedicated deployments.
[04:30] Lina Gomez: Security — SSO, audit logs, and KMS?
[04:33] Jordan Lee: We support SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration (customers can bring their own keys). We'll attach the SOC2 and ISO docs in the follow-up.
[04:42] Aisha Patel: Great. Also need IP allowlist details.
[04:44] Jordan Lee: We'll include that in the security pack.
[04:47] Priya Kapoor: Quick aside on quality regression — Redwood Optimize can run periodic evals against a test prompt set and alert if any metric drops after model changes. Good for POC to detect regressions as you tweak params.
[04:58] Marcus Chen: Can we see console cost visibility?
[05:00] Priya Kapoor: Switching to console demo — per-route token breakdown, per-token latency heatmaps, and a model selector. Here you can set autoscale and burst rules so you don't overpay during spikes.
[05:15] [console demo sounds] Priya Kapoor: Also we surfaced a recommended batching config based on your qps to improve throughput for short responses — useful for cost optimization.
[05:26] Lina Gomez: One concern — consistency of streaming under mobile networks.
[05:30] Priya Kapoor: Good point. For lossy networks we recommend shorter chunks, local buffering, and client-side dedupe. Another pattern is to stream a short summary first and then lazily stream full detail as it becomes available.
[05:45] Marcus Chen: Can we implement a progressive reveal? yes we'd like that pattern.
[05:48] Priya Kapoor: Exactly — early tokens for immediate UX and follow-up details continue.
[05:52] Noah Rivera: On retries, do you log idempotency keys so we can reconcile duplicates?
[05:56] Jordan Lee: Audit logs capture request ids and idempotency keys. We'll show an example in the logs we send.
[06:02] Aisha Patel: Any limitations around max concurrency per API key?
[06:06] Marta Ruiz: Hosted tier has soft concurrency limits per account; for scale we recommend Dedicated reservations. But you can request increases and we can suggest safe fanout patterns.
[06:17] Marcus Chen: Ok we're interested in a short POC — main objectives: keep latency under 300ms for single-turn responses, cost under $0.02 per conversation on average, and maintain privacy of logs.
[06:29] Jordan Lee: Great — we'll scope the POC benchmarks around those SLOs. We'll also include a fallback plan.
[06:35] Priya Kapoor: For the benchmark I'll test three configs: 1) high-quality base, 2) compact quantized model, 3) policy fallback with smaller model. We'll measure throughput, p95 latency, and avg tokens per session.
[06:49] Marcus Chen: Sounds good. A couple quick questions from Lina: does Redwood expose token-level breakdown over time?
[06:55] Priya Kapoor: Yes, per-route token histogram with time-series; helpful to identify prompt bloat.
[07:02] Lina Gomez: And about prompt caching again — how do we warm the cache?
[07:06] Priya Kapoor: Cache warms on repeated prefixes. For synthetic warm-up you can replay a handful of representative requests and the runtime will populate the KV cache. We'll also show a small script to do that.
[07:18] Noah Rivera: Any gotchas with streaming and WebSockets through corporate proxies?
[07:22] Marta Ruiz: Some proxies cut long-lived connections; recommended: use short lived streams and chunking, or use the polling fallback if proxies block WS. We capture these as error classes in our SDK.
[07:35] Aisha Patel: How about data retention and ability to opt-out logs?
[07:38] Jordan Lee: Hosted retains minimal logs by default for billing; for PII-sensitive flows we recommend Private deployment or customer-managed retention — we can support deletion on request.
[07:48] Marcus Chen: Ok anything else on model params we should monitor?
[07:51] Priya Kapoor: Keep eye on temperature, top_p, length penalties and repetition penalty for chat loops. Also watch stop sequences to limit hallucinations.
[07:59] Lina Gomez: We have an internal policy of not exceeding 4k tokens per convo — is that enforced by Redwood?
[08:03] Jordan Lee: You can configure hard token caps per route in the console. We'll include a sample policy.
[08:10] Priya Kapoor: Quick demo of a failure and fallback: I simulate a 503 on the primary model, stream closes, our SDK reattempts with exponential backoff and then routes to compact-v1 as configured. Watch the timeline in the trace.
[08:22] [demo noise] Priya Kapoor: After failover you can see a brief quality delta but response is still sensible.
[08:30] Marcus Chen: That tradeoff is acceptable for maintaining uptime.
[08:33] Jordan Lee: Ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[08:36] Jordan Lee: Jordan to send pricing/security; Priya to run the benchmark; BlueCanvas to share logs and SSO details. Schedule POC kickoff for next week.
[08:44] Noah Rivera: Thanks folks, good session.
[08:46] Marcus Chen: Thanks, appreciate the quick demo.
[08:48] Jordan Lee: We'll follow up with calendar invite and links. Thanks everyone.

[END OF TRANSCRIPT]
notes: Customer emphasized latency SLO (p50 <300ms) and cost target; SE to run three-variant benchmark; security docs required before POC. Some transcription artifacts: 'K V cash' for KV cache, 'redwood' sometimes lowercase in transcription.
